Intuitively,\\\\nwhen p is not exactly half, one model receives more requests\\\\nthan the other. This larger portion of requests have a longer\\\\nqueueing delay, which leads to the higher overall mean la-\\\\ntency.\\\\nFor the model-parallel case, the requests to both models\\\\nmerged to a single Poisson Process with rate λ. For pipeline\\\\nparallelism, suppose the latency for a single input to be Ds\\\\nand the maximum stage latency to be Dm, then the average\\\\nlatency would be\\\\nWpipeline = Ds +\\\\nλD2\\\\nm\\\\n2(1−λDm).\\\\n0.0\\\\n0.5\\\\n1.0\\\\n1.5\\\\n2.0\\\\nD\\\\n1.0\\\\n1.2\\\\n1.4\\\\nFigure 10: Maximal communication overhead α and uneven\\\\npartition overhead β satisfy Wpipeline ≤Wsimple as a function\\\\nof total utilization λD.\\\\nSuppose there is no model-parallel overhead, then Ds =\\\\n2Dm = D. Let’s ﬁrst consider the case where p = 1/2 (Fig. 2a).\\\\nWe have\\\\nWsimple = D+\\\\nλD2\\\\n4−2λD,\\\\nWpipeline = D+\\\\nλD2\\\\n8−4λD.\\\\nIn this case, the waiting time for model-parallel execution is\\\\nhalf of the simple placement waiting time, as shown in the\\\\nvertical lines in Fig. 2a. When the p is not 1/2, Wsimple will\\\\nincrease while Wpipeline will stay the same, so the gap between\\\\nWsimple and Wpipeline will be even larger, as in Fig. 2c.\\\\nNext, we consider the case where model parallelism in-\\\\ncurs overhead. We measure the two types of overheads in\\\\n§3.3 separately: With the overhead from communication,\\\\nDs = 2Dm = αD, where α ≥1 is the overhead factor. With\\\\nthe overhead from uneven stages, we suppose Ds = D still\\\\nholds, but Dm = βD/2 where β ≥1 is the overhead factor.\\\\nTo keep Wpipeline ≤Wsimple, we can get the maximal α and\\\\nβ as a function of the total utilization λD separately and we\\\\nvisualize the function in Fig. 10. When the utilization is high,\\\\nthe beneﬁt of statistical multiplexing diminishes, and thus\\\\nthe overhead needs to be low, as in §3.2. On the other hand,\\\\nwhen the utilization is very low, most requests will not be\\\\nqueued, and thus the communication overhead α needs to\\\\nbe low to keep the processing latency to be low. Note that\\\\nthe maximal overhead here is based on a uniform Poisson ar-\\\\nrival distribution. A more bursty or more non-uniform arrival\\\\ndistribution will make the simple placement performs worse\\\\nand make the model-parallelism placement outperforms the\\\\nsimple replication placement with even higher overhead.\\\\n4\\\\nMethod\\\\nFrom §3, we can see that there are several key challenges to\\\\neffectively utilize model parallelism for deep learning serving:\\\\n6\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 7 ===\\\\nController\\\\nHTTP Requests\\\\nModel a\\\\nModel b\\\\nModel c\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nModel Parallel Runtime\\\\nModel a\\\\nModel d\\\\nModel e\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nModel Parallel Runtime\\\\nModel f\\\\nModel g\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nModel Parallel Runtime\\\\nGroup 1\\\\nGroup 2\\\\nGroup 3\\\\nFigure 11: AlpaServe Runtime System Architecture\\\\n• Derive efﬁcient model parallel strategies for inference to\\\\nreduce the overhead of model parallelism. Speciﬁcally,\\\\nﬁnd a partitioning strategy that minimizes the stage im-\\\\nbalance for inter-operator parallelism.\\\\n• Determine model-parallel placements according to the\\\\narrival pattern to maximize SLO attainment.\\\\nWe built AlpaServe to speciﬁcally tackle these challenges.\\\\nThe runtime architecture of AlpaServe is shown in Fig. 11. Al-\\\\npaServe utilizes a centralized controller to dispatch requests to\\\\ndifferent groups. Each group hosts several model replicas on\\\\na shared model-parallel runtime. This section describes the ar-\\\\nchitecture of AlpaServe and the key algorithms for efﬁciently\\\\nleveraging model parallelism in a model serving system.\\\\n4.1\\\\nAutomatic Parallelization for Inference\\\\nSince different parallelization conﬁgurations have different\\\\nlatency and throughput trade-offs, we need to enumerate mul-\\\\ntiple possible conﬁgurations for every single model and let the\\\\nplacement algorithm choose the best combination for all mod-\\\\nels in the whole cluster. Therefore, given a model, AlpaServe\\\\nﬁrst runs an auto-parallelization compiler with various con-\\\\nstraints to generate a list of possible conﬁgurations. We build\\\\nseveral extensions on top of an existing auto parallelization\\\\ntraining system, Alpa [48], to make it suitable for generating\\\\nserving parallelization strategies. Alpa includes two passes\\\\nfor generating efﬁcient model parallel partitions: inter-op pass\\\\nand intra-op pass. The inter-op pass uses a dynamic program-\\\\nming (DP) algorithm to ﬁgure out the optimal inter-op parallel\\\\nplan, and it calls the intra-op pass for each potential pipeline\\\\nstage, which is formulated as an integer linear programming\\\\n(ILP) problem, to proﬁle its latency with the optimal intra-\\\\nop parallel plan. In AlpaServe, we keep the two compilation\\\\npasses, but extends both passes for serving.\\\\nThe inter-op pass in Alpa optimizes the overall pipeline\\\\nexecution latency, which includes the time of forward and\\\\nbackward propagation and weight synchronization. However,\\\\nin serving workloads, only forward propagation is being exe-\\\\ncuted and there is no need for weight synchronization. There-\\\\nfore, we reformulate the dynamic programming in AlpaServe\\\\nto merely focus on minimizing the maximal stage latency.\\\\nSpeciﬁcally, denote F(s,k) to be the maximum latency when\\\\nslicing layers 1 to k into s stages. We can derive F as\\\\nF(s,k) = min\\\\n1≤i≤k{max{F(s−1,i−1),latency(i,k)}},\\\\nwhere latency(i,k) denotes the latency of a stage composes\\\\nof layer i to k. In Alpa, the latency function of all possible\\\\nO(K2) combinations is being proﬁled by the intra-op pass\\\\nbecause of the complicated dependency between forward and\\\\nbackward passes. In AlpaServe, because the pipeline stages\\\\nonly perform forward propagation and only communicate\\\\nintermediate results once between layer boundaries, we can\\\\naccelerate the proﬁling by only proﬁling K layers and letting\\\\nlatency(i,k) to be the sum of the latencies for layer i to k.\\\\nThis acceleration enables us to efﬁciently enumerate different\\\\ninter- and intra-op device partition setups and generate a list\\\\nof parallel strategies for the placement algorithm in §4.2.\\\\nFor the intra-op pass, we extend the ILP in Alpa to drop\\\\nall conﬁgurations that use data parallelism. For serving work-\\\\nloads, because there is no need for weight synchronization,\\\\ndata parallelism can be achieved by the replication placement.\\\\nWe leave the decision of whether to replicate a model to the\\\\nplacement algorithm in §4.2.\\\\n4.2\\\\nPlacement Algorithm\\\\nGiven a set of models and a ﬁxed cluster, AlpaServe parti-\\\\ntions the cluster into several groups of devices. Each group\\\\nof devices selects a subset of models to serve using a shared\\\\nmodel-parallel conﬁguration. Different groups can hold the\\\\nsame model as replicas. The requests for a model are dis-\\\\npatched to the groups with the requested model replica. We\\\\ncall a speciﬁc cluster group partition, model selection, and\\\\nparallel conﬁguration as a placement. Our goal is to ﬁnd a\\\\nplacement that maximizes the SLO attainment.\\\\nHowever, ﬁnding the optimal placement is a difﬁcult combi-\\\\nnatorial optimization problem. The overall placement conﬁg-\\\\nuration space grows exponentially with the number of devices\\\\nand the number of models. To make things worse, the objec-\\\\ntive “SLO attainment” has no simple analytical formula for\\\\nan arbitrary arrival distribution. Existing tools and approxima-\\\\ntions from queueing theory can only analyze simple cases in\\\\n§3.4 and cannot model more complex situations [41]. There-\\\\nfore, we resort to a simulator-guided greedy algorithm that\\\\ncalls a simulator to compute SLO attainment.\\\\nTo compute the SLO attainment with a given set of requests\\\\nand placement, in AlpaServe, we assume we know the arrival\\\\nprocess in advance. Although short-term burstiness is impos-\\\\nsible to predict, the arrival pattern over longer timescales (e.g.,\\\\nhours or days) is often predictable [43]. Given this predictabil-\\\\nity, AlpaServe either directly uses the history request traces\\\\nor ﬁts a distribution from the trace and resamples new traces\\\\nfrom the distribution as the input workload to the simulator\\\\nto compute the SLO attainment.\\\\nWe design a two-level placement algorithm: Given a cluster\\\\ngroup partition and a shared model-parallel conﬁguration for\\\\neach group, Algorithm 1 uses a simulator-guided greedy algo-\\\\nrithm to decide which models to select for each group. Then,\\\\nAlgorithm 2 enumerates various potential cluster partitions\\\\nand parallel conﬁgurations and compares the SLO attainment\\\\nfrom Algorithm 1 to determine the optimal placement.\\\\n7\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 8 ===\\\\nAlgorithm 1 Simulator-Guided Greedy Model Selection.\\\\nInput: Model list M, device group list G, group parallel con-\\\\nﬁgurations P, workload W, beam size k (default = 1).\\\\nOutput: The model selection best_sel.\\\\nbest_sel ←/0\\\\nbeam_sels ←{/0}\\\\nwhile true do\\\\nnew_sels ←/0\\\\nfor sel ∈beam_sels do\\\\nfor (m,(g, p)) ∈M ×(G,P) do\\\\n// Parallelize the model as in §4.1.\\\\nmparallelized ←parallelize(m,g, p)\\\\nsel′ ←sel.add_model_to_group(mparallelized,g)\\\\nif sel′ is in memory constraint then\\\\nsel′.slo_attainment ←simulate(sel′,W)\\\\nnew_sels.append(sel′)\\\\nif new_sels = /0 then\\\\nbreak\\\\nbeam_sels ←top-k_SLO_attainment(new_sels)\\\\nsel∗←pick_highest_SLO_attainment(beam_sels)\\\\nif sel∗.slo_att > best_sel.slo_att then\\\\nbest_sel ←sel∗\\\\nreturn best_sel\\\\nGiven a cluster group partition with a ﬁxed model-parallel\\\\nconﬁguration for each group, Algorithm 1 selects model repli-\\\\ncas iteratively as a beam search algorithm: At each iteration,\\\\nit enumerates all possible (model, group) pairs, parallelizes\\\\nthe model on the device group with the algorithms in §4.1,\\\\nand checks whether the model can be put on the group under\\\\nthe memory constraint. For all valid selections, it runs the\\\\nsimulator and computes SLO attainment. It then picks the\\\\ntop-k solutions and enters the next iteration. The algorithm\\\\nterminates when no more replicas can be put into any groups.\\\\nThe complexity of Algorithm 1 is O(MGRSB), where M\\\\nis the number of models, G is the number of groups, R is\\\\nthe number of replicas we can put according to the memory\\\\nconstraint, S is the number of requests in the workload (the\\\\nsimulation time is proportional to the number of the requests)\\\\nand B is the beam size. It runs reasonably fast for our medium-\\\\nscale cluster when the number of requests is small. When the\\\\nnumber of requests is very large, we propose another heuristic\\\\nto accelerate: Instead of using the simulator to evaluate all\\\\n(model, group) pairs at each iteration, we can run the simu-\\\\nlator only once and place a model with the most unserved\\\\nrequests in an available group with the lowest utilization. This\\\\nreduces the time complexity to O((M +G)RS). We ﬁnd this\\\\nheuristic gives solutions with SLO attainment higher than\\\\n98% of the SLO attainment get by the original algorithm in\\\\nour benchmarks.\\\\nAlgorithm 2 enumerates different group partitions and\\\\nmodel-parallel conﬁgurations and picks the best one via mul-\\\\nAlgorithm 2 Enumeration-Based Group Partition and Model-\\\\nParallel Conﬁguration Selection.\\\\nInput: Model list M, cluster C, workload W.\\\\nOutput: The placement best_plm.\\\\nbest_plm ←/0\\\\nB ←get_potential_model_buckets(M)\\\\nfor (B1,B2,...,Bk) ∈B do\\\\nH ←get_potential_device_buckets(C,B,k)\\\\nfor (H1,H2,...,Hk) ∈H do\\\\n// Get the placement for each bucket individually.\\\\nfor i from 1 to k do\\\\nplm∗\\\\ni ←/0\\\\nG ←get_potential_group_partitions(Hi)\\\\nfor G ∈G do\\\\nP ←get_potential_parallel_conﬁgs(G)\\\\nfor P ∈P do\\\\nplm ←greedy_selection(Bi,G,P,W)\\\\nif plm.slo_att > plm∗\\\\ni .slo_att then\\\\nplm∗\\\\ni ←plm\\\\nplm∗←concat(plm∗\\\\n1,...,plm∗\\\\nk)\\\\nif plm∗.slo_att > best_plm.slo_att then\\\\nbest_plm ←plm∗\\\\nreturn best_plm\\\\ntiple calls to Algorithm 1. When designing Algorithm 2,\\\\nthe ﬁrst phenomenon we notice is that putting small and\\\\nlarge models in the same group causes convoy effects, where\\\\nthe requests of small models have to wait for the requests\\\\nof large models and miss the SLO. Therefore, in Algo-\\\\nrithm 2, we ﬁrst cluster models into model buckets. Each\\\\nbucket contains a set of models with relatively similar sizes\\\\nand every model is assigned to one and only one bucket.\\\\nSpeciﬁcally, the function get_potential_model_buckets\\\\nreturns all the possible model bucket partitions that sepa-\\\\nrate models whose latency difference is larger than a thresh-\\\\nold into different disjoint buckets. We then enumerate all\\\\nthe potential ways to assign the devices to each bucket in\\\\nget_potential_device_buckets.\\\\nBecause different buckets include a disjoint set of models,\\\\nwe can then ﬁgure out the optimal placement for each bucket\\\\nindividually. For each bucket, we enumerate possible ways\\\\nto partition the devices in the bucket into several groups in\\\\nget_potential_group_partitions and enumerate the po-\\\\ntential parallel conﬁgurations for each group with the method\\\\nin get_potential_parallel_configs. We then call Al-\\\\ngorithm 1 with greedy_placement to place models in the\\\\nmodel bucket to the groups in the device bucket. We send the\\\\nwhole workload W to Algorithm 1, which ignores the requests\\\\nthat hit the models outside of the current bucket. Finally, a\\\\ncomplete solution is got by concatenating the solutions for\\\\nall buckets. The algorithm returns the best solution it ﬁnds\\\\nduring the enumerative search process.\\\\n8\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 9 ===\\\\nEnumerating all possible choices can be slow, so we use\\\\nthe following heuristics to prune the search space. Intuitively,\\\\nwe want the different buckets to serve a similar number of\\\\nrequests per second. Therefore, we eliminate the bucket con-\\\\nﬁgurations with high discrepancies in the estimated num-\\\\nber of requests it can serve per second for each bucket.\\\\nAdditionally, in get_potential_group_partitions and\\\\nget_potential_parallel_configs, we assume all groups\\\\nhave the same size and the same parallel conﬁgurations except\\\\nfor the last group which is used when the number of devices\\\\nis not divisible by the group size.\\\\n4.3\\\\nRuntime Scheduling\\\\nWe use a simple policy to dispatch and schedule the requests at\\\\nruntime. All requests are sent to a centralized controller. The\\\\ncontroller dispatches each request to the group with the short-\\\\nest queue length. Each group manages a ﬁrst-come-ﬁrst-serve\\\\nqueue. When a group receives a request, it checks whether\\\\nit can serve the request under SLO and rejects the request if\\\\nit cannot. This is possible because the execution time of a\\\\nDNN model is very predictable and can be got in advance by\\\\nproﬁling [17]. In most of our experiments, we do not include\\\\nadvanced runtime policies such as batching [17], swapping,\\\\nand preemption [18]. These techniques are complementary to\\\\nmodel parallelism. Nevertheless, we discuss how they ﬁt into\\\\nour system.\\\\nBatching. Batching multiple requests of the same model to-\\\\ngether can increase the GPU utilization and thus increase the\\\\nthroughput of a serving system. In our system, we do ﬁnd\\\\nbatching is helpful, but the gain is limited. This is because we\\\\nmainly target large models and a small batch size can already\\\\nfully saturate the GPU, which is veriﬁed in §6.5. To isolate\\\\nthe beneﬁts of model parallelism and make the results more\\\\nexplainable, we decide to disable any batching in this paper\\\\nexcept for the experiments in §6.5.\\\\nPreemption. The optimal scheduling decision often depends\\\\non future arrivals, and leveraging preemption can help cor-\\\\nrect previous suboptimal decisions. The ﬁrst-come-ﬁrst-serve\\\\npolicy may result in convoy effects when models with signiﬁ-\\\\ncantly different execution times are placed in the same group.\\\\nWe anticipate a least-slack-time-ﬁrst policy with preemption\\\\ncan alleviate the problems [10].\\\\nSwapping. The loading overheads from the CPU or Disk to\\\\nGPU memory are signiﬁcant for large models, which is the\\\\ntarget of this paper, so we do not implement swapping in Al-\\\\npaServe. We assume all models are placed on the GPUs. This\\\\nis often required due to tight SLOs and high rates, especially\\\\nfor large models. The placement of models in AlpaServe can\\\\nbe updated in the periodic re-placement (e.g., every 24 hours).\\\\nFault tolerance. While the current design of AlpaServe does\\\\nnot have fault tolerance as a focus, we acknowledge several\\\\npotential new challenges for fault tolerance: With model par-\\\\nallelism, the failure of a single GPU could cause the entire\\\\ngroup to malfunction. Additionally, the use of a centralized\\\\ncontroller presents a single point of failure.\\\\n5\\\\nImplementation\\\\nWe implement a real system and a simulator for AlpaServe\\\\nwith about 4k lines of code in Python. The real system is\\\\nimplemented on top of an existing model-parallel training sys-\\\\ntem, Alpa [48]. We extend its auto-parallelization algorithms\\\\nfor inference settings to get the model-parallel strategies. We\\\\nthen launch an Alpa runtime for each group and dispatch\\\\nrequests to these groups via a centralized controller.\\\\nThe simulator is a continuous-time, discrete-event simula-\\\\ntor [35]. The simulator maintains a global clock and simulates\\\\nall requests and model executions on the cluster. Because the\\\\nsimulator only models discrete events, it is orders of mag-\\\\nnitude faster than the real experiments. The ﬁdelity of the\\\\nsimulator is very high because of the predictability of DNN\\\\nmodel execution, which is veriﬁed in §6.1.\\\\n6\\\\nEvaluation\\\\nIn this section, we evaluate AlpaServe’s serving ability under\\\\na variety of model and workload conditions. The evaluation is\\\\nconducted on a range of model sizes, including those that do\\\\nand do not ﬁt into a single GPU, and we show that AlpaServe\\\\nconsistently outperforms strong baselines across all model\\\\nsizes. In addition, we evaluate the robustness of AlpaServe\\\\nagainst changing arrival patterns and do ablation studies of our\\\\nproposed techniques. Evaluation results show that AlpaServe\\\\ncan greatly improve various performance metrics. Speciﬁcally,\\\\nAlpaServe can choose to save up to 2.3× devices, handle 10×\\\\nhigher rates, 6× more burstiness, or 2.5× more stringent SLO,\\\\nwhile meeting the latency SLOs for over 99% requests.\\\\n6.1\\\\nExperiment Setup\\\\nCluster testbed. We deploy AlpaServe on a cluster with 8\\\\nnodes and 64 GPUs. Each node is an AWS EC2 p3.16xlarge\\\\ninstance with 8 NVIDIA Tesla V100 (16GB) GPUs.\\\\nModel setup. Since Transformer [42] is the default backbone\\\\nfor large models, we choose two representative large Trans-\\\\nformer model families: BERT [12] and GShard MoE [23]\\\\nfor evaluation.2 In ML practice, the large model weights are\\\\nusually pretrained and then ﬁnetuned into different versions\\\\nfor different tasks. Hence, for each model family, we select\\\\nseveral most commonly used model sizes [3], and then create\\\\nmultiple model instances at each size for experimentation.\\\\nAlso, we design some model sets to test the serving systems\\\\nunder different model conditions; details about model sizes,\\\\ntheir inference latency on testbed GPUs, and the number of\\\\nmodel instances in each model set are provided in Tab. 1.\\\\nMetrics. We use SLO attainment as the major evaluation met-\\\\nric. Additionally,\\\\nwe conduct experiments on cluster testbed for results in §6.3.\\\\n6.2\\\\nEnd-to-end Results with Real Workloads\\\\nIn this section, we compare AlpaServe against baseline meth-\\\\nods on publicly available real traces.\\\\nWorkloads. We use two real traces: Microsoft Azure func-\\\\ntion trace 2019 (MAF1) [37] and 2021 (MAF2) [47]. They\\\\nwere originally collected from Azure serverless function in-\\\\nvocations in two weeks, and have been repurposed for ML\\\\nserving research [2,21]. The two traces exhibit distinct trafﬁc\\\\npatterns. In MAF1, each function receives steady and dense\\\\nincoming requests with gradually changing rates; in MAF2,\\\\nthe trafﬁc is very bursty and is distributed across functions\\\\nin a highly skewed way – some function receives orders of\\\\nmagnitude more requests than others. Note that most previous\\\\nworks [17] are evaluated on MAF1 only. Since there are more\\\\nfunctions than models, following previous work [2,21], given\\\\na model set from Tab. 1, we round-robin functions to models\\\\nto generate trafﬁc for each model.\\\\nSetup. SLO attainment depends on many factors. For each\\\\nmetric (1) - (4) mentioned in §6.1, we set a default value, e.g.,\\\\nthe default SLO is set as tight as 5× inference latency (SLO\\\\nScale=5). This forms a default setting, given which, we then\\\\nvary one variable (while ﬁxing others) at a time and observe\\\\nhow it affects the resulting SLO attainment. To change the\\\\ntwo variables (3) and (4), which characterize trafﬁc patterns,\\\\nwe follow Clockwork [17] and Inferline [6] and slice the\\\\noriginal traces into time windows, and ﬁt the arrivals in each\\\\ntime window with a Gamma Process parameterized by rate\\\\nand coefﬁcient of variance (CV). By scaling the rate and CV\\\\nand resampling from the processes, we can control the rate\\\\nand burstiness, respectively.\\\\nBaselines. We compare AlpaServe to two baseline methods:\\\\n(1) Selective Replication (SR): use AlpaServe’s placement al-\\\\ngorithm without model parallelism, which mimics the policy\\\\nof a wide range of existing serving systems [7,39]; (2) Clock-\\\\nwork++: an improved version of the state-of-the-art model\\\\nserving system Clockwork [17]. The original Clockwork con-\\\\ntinuously swaps models into and out of GPUs. This helps for\\\\nvery small models (e.g., w/ several million parameters) but\\\\nincurs signiﬁcant swapping overheads on larger models. For\\\\nfair comparisons, we implement Clockwork++ in our simula-\\\\ntor, which swaps models following Clockwork’s replacement\\\\nstrategy at the boundary of every two windows3 of the trace\\\\nusing SR’s algorithm, but assuming zero swapping overheads.\\\\nWe believe it represents a hypothetical upper bound of Clock-\\\\nwork’s performance. Since all the baselines can only support\\\\nmodels that can ﬁt into one GPU memory,4 we use model set\\\\nS1, S2 and S3 from Tab. 1 in this experiment.\\\\nSLO attainment vs. cluster size. Although enumerating par-\\\\nallelism strategies and selecting the best can improve per-\\\\nformance, it still remains a substantial gap compared to Al-\\\\npaServe. This means that the traditional way of using ded-\\\\nicated GPUs to serve large models is not ideal. We check\\\\nthe solution of AlpaServe and ﬁnd it slices the cluster evenly\\\\ninto two groups, each with the (4, 8) inter-/intra-op parallel\\\\nconﬁguration, and groups the models in a way that balances\\\\nthe requests between two groups. This further proves that our\\\\nmotivation in §3.1 still holds for extremely large models. By\\\\nspace-sharing the devices, AlpaServe can exploit new oppor-\\\\ntunities for statistical multiplexing, which is advantageous for\\\\nbursty workloads but largely under-explored by prior work.\\\\n6.4\\\\nRobustness to Changing Trafﬁc Patterns\\\\nUntil now, AlpaServe’s good performance is based on the\\\\nassumption we make in its placement algorithm that we know\\\\nthe arrival process in advance. In practice, the arrival process\\\\ncan be approximated using historical traces but the unavoid-\\\\nable real-world variance may make the prediction inaccurate.\\\\nIn this experiment, we study how AlpaServe performs if the\\\\ntrafﬁc patterns change.\\\\nWe reuse the same setting for S2@MAF1 in §6.2, but this\\\\ntime for AlpaServe and SR, we randomly slice two one-hour\\\\ntraces from MAF1, one is what their algorithms are assumed,\\\\nwhile the other one is used as the actual arrival process. While\\\\n5Uniform split yielded similar results.\\\\nfor Clockwork++, we still run its algorithm directly on the\\\\nactual arrival process to respect its online nature. Similarly,\\\\nwe vary different factors and compute the SLO attainment for\\\\neach system. We repeat the experiments three times and show\\\\nthe average results in Fig. 14.\\\\nUnsurprisingly, SR’s performance drops signiﬁcantly when\\\\ntrafﬁc changes. By contrast, AlpaServe maintains good per-\\\\nformance and still outperforms Clockwork++, an online ad-\\\\njustment algorithm, using a static placement generated from\\\\nsubstantially different trafﬁc patterns. This conﬁrms that, in\\\\nface of highly-dynamic trafﬁc patterns, statistical multiplex-\\\\ning with model parallelism is a simple and better alternative\\\\nthan existing replication- or replacement-based algorithms.\\\\n6.5\\\\nBeneﬁts of Dynamic Batching\\\\nBatching is a common optimization in other serving sys-\\\\ntems [17, 29, 30] and the choice of batch size is critical to\\\\nthe performance because it can increase GPU utilization and\\\\nthus increase the system throughput. However, in large model\\\\nscenarios, the beneﬁt of batching is limited mainly due to\\\\ntwo reasons. First, for large models, a small batch size will\\\\nsaturate the GPU, which means there is little gain to batching\\\\nmore requests. Second, the execution latency grows linearly\\\\nwith the batch size [39], so when the SLO is tight (say SLO\\\\nScale is less than 2), batching is simply not a choice.\\\\nTo isolate the beneﬁts of model parallelism and make the\\\\nresults more explainable, we decide to disable any batching\\\\nin other experiments but prove that the batching strategy is\\\\npurely orthogonal to the scope of this paper in this subsection.\\\\nTo prove this, we implement a standard batching algorithm in\\\\nAlpaServe and evaluate its performance.\\\\nBatching strategy. When a request arrives, it will get exe-\\\\ncuted immediately if any device group is available. Otherwise,\\\\nit will be put into a per-model requests queue for batching.\\\\nWhen a device group becomes idle, it will choose a model\\\\nwhich has a replica on it and batch as many requests as possi-\\\\nble from the requests queue of the model while satisfying the\\\\nSLO requirements.\\\\nSetup. As the model size increases, the potential beneﬁt of\\\\nbatching decreases. Therefore, we choose to evaluate model\\\\nset S1. We generate a synthetic Gamma Process trafﬁc with\\\\nan average rate of 4 requests/s and a CV of 4 for each model.\\\\nSLO attainment. Fig. 15 (left) shows the SLO attainment\\\\nachieved by AlpaServe with different maximum batch size set-\\\\ntings under various SLO scales. When the SLO requirement\\\\nis tight, any batching will violate the SLO so there is no gain\\\\nwith batching enabled. Also, although we choose to serve the\\\\nsmallest model in Tab. 1, a small batch size like 2 combined\\\\nwith a long sequence length of 2048 already saturates the\\\\nGPU, so a larger maximum batch size brings no performance\\\\nimprovement. Fig. 15 (right) compares the improvement for\\\\nAlpaServe and Clockwork++ with our batching algorithm\\\\n12\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 13 ===\\\\n10\\\\n20\\\\n30\\\\n40\\\\n50\\\\n#devices\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\n0.002\\\\n0.004\\\\n0.006\\\\n0.008\\\\nRate Scale\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n6\\\\n8\\\\nCV Scale\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n6\\\\n8\\\\n10\\\\nSLO Scale\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\nSLO Attainment (%)\\\\nAlpaServe\\\\nClockwork++\\\\nSR\\\\nFigure 14: The actual arrival trafﬁc for AlpaServe and SR is different from what their algorithms are assumed, while Clockwork++\\\\nruns directly on the actual trafﬁc.\\\\n0.0\\\\n2.5\\\\n5.0\\\\n7.5\\\\n10.0\\\\n12.5\\\\nSLO Scale\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\nAlpaServe\\\\nAlpaServe (mb=2)\\\\nAlpaServe (mb=4)\\\\nAlpaServe (mb=8)\\\\nAlpaServe (mb=16)\\\\n0.0\\\\n2.5\\\\n5.0\\\\n7.5\\\\n10.0\\\\n12.5\\\\nSLO Scale\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\nAlpaServe\\\\nClockwork++\\\\nAlpaServe (mb=2)\\\\nClockwork++ (mb=2)\\\\nSLO Attainment (%)\\\\nFigure 15: SLO Attainment when batching is enabled. mb=2\\\\nmeans the maximum batch size is 2.\\\\nenabled.6 When the SLO requirement becomes loose, both\\\\nAlpaServe and Clockwork++ have better SLO attainment to\\\\nsome extent. We show that the auto-\\\\nparallelization ability allows AlpaServe to not only gener-\\\\nalize to arbitrary model architectures but even also reduce\\\\nparallelism overheads – hence improved serving performance\\\\n(see §3.3 for more discussion). To see that, typical manual\\\\nmodel-parallel parallelization strategies offered in de facto\\\\nsystems [1, 27, 28] is to assign an equal number of (trans-\\\\nformer) layers to each pipeline stage. These strategies often\\\\nfail to create balanced workloads across distributed GPUs be-\\\\ncause contemporary large models have heterogeneous layers,\\\\nsuch as embedding operations. The extensions introduced in\\\\n§4.1 automatically partition the models at the computational\\\\ngraph level and generate nearly-balanced stages. Empirically,\\\\nas shown in Fig. 16, for 8 pipeline stages, auto-parallelization\\\\nreduces the total overhead by 32.9% and 46.7% for Trans-\\\\nformer 1.3B and 2.6B respectively, which is necessary for\\\\nachieving good serving performance when model parallelism\\\\nis used for serving.\\\\nEffectiveness of the placement algorithm. We now test the\\\\neffectiveness of our placement algorithm on a synthetic work-\\\\n6SR is left out to make the ﬁgure clearer as it is worse than Clockwork++.\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\nNumber of GPUs\\\\n0.100\\\\n0.125\\\\n0.150\\\\n0.175\\\\n0.200\\\\n0.225\\\\n0.250\\\\nLatency (s)\\\\nCompuation\\\\nCommunication Overhead\\\\nUneven Partition Overhead\\\\n(a) Transformer 1.3B.\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\nNumber of GPUs\\\\n0.20\\\\n0.22\\\\n0.24\\\\n0.26\\\\n0.28\\\\n0.30\\\\nLatency (s)\\\\nCompuation\\\\nCommunication Overhead\\\\nUneven Partition Overhead\\\\n(b) Transformer 2.6B.\\\\nFigure 16: Comparison of the model parallel overhead be-\\\\ntween manual partition (lighter color) and the partition found\\\\nby the automatic algorithm (darker color).\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\n#models\\\\n60\\\\n65\\\\n70\\\\n75\\\\n80\\\\n85\\\\n90\\\\n95\\\\n100\\\\nRound robin\\\\nGreedy placement\\\\nGreedy placement + Group partitioning\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\n120\\\\nRate Scale\\\\n60\\\\n65\\\\n70\\\\n75\\\\n80\\\\n85\\\\n90\\\\n95\\\\n100\\\\nRound robin\\\\nGreedy placement\\\\nGreedy placement + Group partitioning\\\\nSLO Attainment (%)\\\\nFigure 17: Ablation study of placement algorithms.\\\\nload. There has been a proliferation of\\\\nmodel serving systems recently. These range from general-\\\\n13\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 14 ===\\\\npurpose production-grade systems like TensorFlow Serv-\\\\ning [30] and NVIDIA Triton [29], which are widely used but\\\\ndo not provide any support for automatic placement or latency\\\\nconstraints. They also include systems that are optimized for\\\\nsingle-model serving [45] or serving of speciﬁc classes of\\\\nmodels (e.g., transformers) [14,45,49]. AlpaServe targets a\\\\nbroader set of models and features than these systems.\\\\nFor SLO-aware, distributed serving, most serving systems\\\\nignore placement-level interactions between models. Clock-\\\\nwork [17], for instance, primarily focuses on predictability;\\\\nwhen scheduling, it greedily loads and executes models on\\\\navailable GPUs. For large models, loading model weights\\\\ncan easily overwhelm practical SLOs. Other systems like\\\\nClipper [7] and DVABatch [8] also do not reason about the\\\\nlatencies of co-located models.\\\\nNexus [39] is very related to our work in that it exam-\\\\nines the placement of models; however, Nexus is an example\\\\nof a system that takes the traditional replication approach\\\\ndescribed in §3 and, thus, misses a broad class of potential\\\\nparallelization strategies that we explore in this paper.\\\\nInference optimizations for large models. AlpaServe is\\\\ncomplementary to another large body of work on optimiza-\\\\ntions for inference over large models. These include tech-\\\\nniques like quantization [11], distillation [36], ofﬂoading [1],\\\\nbetter operator parallelism [32], and CUDA kernel optimiza-\\\\ntion [9,22]. Some of these optimizations are intended to stem\\\\nthe tide of increasing model sizes; however, all of these gains\\\\nare partial— the challenge of serving large models has con-\\\\ntinued to escalate rapidly despite these efforts.\\\\nModel parallelism for training. AlpaServe is largely or-\\\\nthogonal to the large body of work on model parallelism in\\\\ntraining [19,27,33,48]. As described in §3, serving presents\\\\na unique set of constraints and opportunities not found in\\\\ntraining workloads. Where these systems do intersect with\\\\nAlpaServe, however, is in their methods for implementing\\\\nmodel parallelism along various dimensions. In particular,\\\\nAlpaServe builds on some of the parallelization techniques\\\\nintroduced in [48].\\\\nResource allocation and multiplexing. The problem of how\\\\nto allocate and multiplex limited resources to a set of incoming\\\\nrequests is one of the oldest topics in computer science [25,\\\\n34]. Rather, the contribution of this paper is a deep empirical\\\\nanalysis of the applications of these ideas to an emerging\\\\nspace: the serving of large models.\\\\n8\\\\nConclusion\\\\nIn this paper, we presented AlpaServe, a system for prediction\\\\nservings of multiple large deep-learning models. The key\\\\ninnovation of AlpaServe is integrating model parallelism into\\\\nmulti-model serving. Because of the inherent overheads of\\\\nmodel parallelism, such parallelism is traditionally applied\\\\nconservatively—reserved for cases where models simply do\\\\nnot ﬁt within a single GPU or execute within the required SLO.\\\\nAlpaServe demonstrates that model parallelism is useful for\\\\nmany other scenarios, quantiﬁes the tradeoffs, and presents\\\\ntechniques to automatically navigate that tradeoff space.\\\\nReferences\\\\n[1] Reza Yazdani Aminabadi, Samyam Rajbhandari, Min-\\\\njia Zhang, Ammar Ahmad Awan, Cheng Li, Du Li, El-\\\\nton Zheng, Jeff Rasley, Shaden Smith, Olatunji Ruwase,\\\\net al. It supports\\\\nhigh-availability applications with runtime features that min-\\\\nimize fault-recovery time, and scheduling policies that re-\\\\nduce the probability of correlated failures. Borg simpliﬁes\\\\nlife for its users by offering a declarative job speciﬁcation\\\\nlanguage, name service integration, real-time job monitor-\\\\ning, and tools to analyze and simulate system behavior.\\\\nWe present a summary of the Borg system architecture\\\\nand features, important design decisions, a quantitative anal-\\\\nysis of some of its policy decisions, and a qualitative ex-\\\\namination of lessons learned from a decade of operational\\\\nexperience with it.\\\\n1.\\\\nIntroduction\\\\nThe cluster management system we internally call Borg ad-\\\\nmits, schedules, starts, restarts, and monitors the full range\\\\nof applications that Google runs. This paper explains how.\\\\nBorg provides three main beneﬁts: it (1) hides the details\\\\nof resource management and failure handling so its users can\\\\nfocus on application development instead; (2) operates with\\\\nvery high reliability and availability, and supports applica-\\\\ntions that do the same; and (3) lets us run workloads across\\\\ntens of thousands of machines effectively. Borg is not the\\\\nﬁrst system to address these issues, but it’s one of the few op-\\\\nerating at this scale, with this degree of resiliency and com-\\\\npleteness. Only a tiny fraction\\\\nof the thousands of worker nodes are shown.\\\\ncluding with a set of qualitative observations we have made\\\\nfrom operating Borg in production for more than a decade.\\\\n2.\\\\nThe user perspective\\\\nBorg’s users are Google developers and system administra-\\\\ntors (site reliability engineers or SREs) that run Google’s\\\\napplications and services. Users submit their work to Borg\\\\nin the form of jobs, each of which consists of one or more\\\\ntasks that all run the same program (binary). Each job runs\\\\nin one Borg cell, a set of machines that are managed as a\\\\nunit. The remainder of this section describes the main fea-\\\\ntures exposed in the user view of Borg.\\\\n2.1\\\\nThe workload\\\\nBorg cells run a heterogenous workload with two main parts.\\\\nThe ﬁrst is long-running services that should “never” go\\\\ndown, and handle short-lived latency-sensitive requests (a\\\\nfew µs to a few hundred ms). Such services are used for\\\\nend-user-facing products such as Gmail, Google Docs, and\\\\nweb search, and for internal infrastructure services (e.g.,\\\\nBigTable). The second is batch jobs that take from a few\\\\nseconds to a few days to complete; these are much less sen-\\\\nsitive to short-term performance ﬂuctuations. The workload\\\\nmix varies across cells, which run different mixes of applica-\\\\ntions depending on their major tenants (e.g., some cells are\\\\nquite batch-intensive), and also varies over time: batch jobs\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 2 ===\\\\ncome and go, and many end-user-facing service jobs see a\\\\ndiurnal usage pattern. Borg is required to handle all these\\\\ncases equally well.\\\\nA representative Borg workload can be found in a publicly-\\\\navailable month-long trace from May 2011 [80], which has\\\\nbeen extensively analyzed (e.g., [68] and [1, 26, 27, 57]).\\\\nMany application frameworks have been built on top of\\\\nBorg over the last few years, including our internal MapRe-\\\\nduce system [23], FlumeJava [18], Millwheel [3], and Pregel\\\\n[59]. Most of these have a controller that submits a master\\\\njob and one or more worker jobs; the ﬁrst two play a similar\\\\nrole to YARN’s application manager [76]. Our distributed\\\\nstorage systems such as GFS [34] and its successor CFS,\\\\nBigtable [19], and Megastore [8] all run on Borg.\\\\nFor this paper, we classify higher-priority Borg jobs as\\\\n“production” (prod) ones, and the rest as “non-production”\\\\n(non-prod). Most long-running server jobs are prod; most\\\\nbatch jobs are non-prod. In a representative cell, prod jobs\\\\nare allocated about 70% of the total CPU resources and rep-\\\\nresent about 60% of the total CPU usage; they are allocated\\\\nabout 55% of the total memory and represent about 85% of\\\\nthe total memory usage. The discrepancies between alloca-\\\\ntion and usage will prove important in §5.5.\\\\n2.2\\\\nClusters and cells\\\\nThe machines in a cell belong to a single cluster, deﬁned by\\\\nthe high-performance datacenter-scale network fabric that\\\\nconnects them. A cluster lives inside a single datacenter\\\\nbuilding, and a collection of buildings makes up a site.1\\\\nA cluster usually hosts one large cell and may have a few\\\\nsmaller-scale test or special-purpose cells. We assiduously\\\\navoid any single point of failure.\\\\nOur median cell size is about 10 k machines after exclud-\\\\ning test cells; some are much larger. The machines in a cell\\\\nare heterogeneous in many dimensions: sizes (CPU, RAM,\\\\ndisk, network), processor type, performance, and capabili-\\\\nties such as an external IP address or ﬂash storage. Borg iso-\\\\nlates users from most of these differences by determining\\\\nwhere in a cell to run tasks, allocating their resources, in-\\\\nstalling their programs and other dependencies, monitoring\\\\ntheir health, and restarting them if they fail.\\\\n2.3\\\\nJobs and tasks\\\\nA Borg job’s properties include its name, owner, and the\\\\nnumber of tasks it has. Jobs can have constraints to force\\\\nits tasks to run on machines with particular attributes such as\\\\nprocessor architecture, OS version, or an external IP address.\\\\nConstraints can be hard or soft; the latter act like preferences\\\\nrather than requirements. The start of a job can be deferred\\\\nuntil a prior one ﬁnishes. A job runs in just one cell.\\\\nEach task maps to a set of Linux processes running in\\\\na container on a machine [62]. The vast majority of the\\\\nBorg workload does not run inside virtual machines (VMs),\\\\n1 There are a few exceptions for each of these relationships.\\\\nbecause we don’t want to pay the cost of virtualization.\\\\nAlso, the system was designed at a time when we had a\\\\nconsiderable investment in processors with no virtualization\\\\nsupport in hardware.\\\\nA task has properties too, such as its resource require-\\\\nments and the task’s index within the job. Most task proper-\\\\nties are the same across all tasks in a job, but can be over-\\\\nridden – e.g., to provide task-speciﬁc command-line ﬂags.\\\\nEach resource dimension (CPU cores, RAM, disk space,\\\\ndisk access rate, TCP ports,2 etc.) is speciﬁed independently\\\\nat ﬁne granularity; we don’t impose ﬁxed-sized buckets or\\\\nslots (§5.4). Borg programs are statically linked to reduce\\\\ndependencies on their runtime environment, and structured\\\\nas packages of binaries and data ﬁles, whose installation is\\\\norchestrated by Borg.\\\\nUsers operate on jobs by issuing remote procedure calls\\\\n(RPCs) to Borg, most commonly from a command-line tool,\\\\nother Borg jobs, or our monitoring systems (§2.6). Most job\\\\ndescriptions are written in the declarative conﬁguration lan-\\\\nguage BCL. This is a variant of GCL [12], which gener-\\\\nates protobuf ﬁles [67], extended with some Borg-speciﬁc\\\\nkeywords. GCL provides lambda functions to allow calcula-\\\\ntions, and these are used by applications to adjust their con-\\\\nﬁgurations to their environment; tens of thousands of BCL\\\\nﬁles are over 1 k lines long, and we have accumulated tens\\\\nof millions of lines of BCL. Borg job conﬁgurations have\\\\nsimilarities to Aurora conﬁguration ﬁles [6].\\\\nFigure 2 illustrates the states that jobs and tasks go\\\\nthrough during their lifetime.\\\\nsubmit + \\\\naccept\\\\nPending\\\\nRunning\\\\nDead\\\\nupdate\\\\nschedule\\\\nupdate\\\\nfinish, fail, kill, lost\\\\nsubmit\\\\nfail, kill, \\\\nlost\\\\nevict\\\\nreject\\\\nFigure 2: The state diagram for both jobs and tasks. Users can\\\\ntrigger submit, kill, and update transitions.\\\\nA user can change the properties of some or all of the\\\\ntasks in a running job by pushing a new job conﬁguration\\\\nto Borg, and then instructing Borg to update the tasks to\\\\nthe new speciﬁcation. This acts as a lightweight, non-atomic\\\\ntransaction that can easily be undone until it is closed (com-\\\\nmitted). Updates are generally done in a rolling fashion, and\\\\na limit can be imposed on the number of task disruptions\\\\n2 Borg manages the available ports on a machine and allocates them to tasks.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 3 ===\\\\n(reschedules or preemptions) an update causes; any changes\\\\nthat would cause more disruptions are skipped.\\\\nSome task updates (e.g., pushing a new binary) will al-\\\\nways require the task to be restarted; some (e.g., increasing\\\\nresource requirements or changing constraints) might make\\\\nthe task no longer ﬁt on the machine, and cause it to be\\\\nstopped and rescheduled; and some (e.g., changing priority)\\\\ncan always be done without restarting or moving the task.\\\\nTasks can ask to be notiﬁed via a Unix SIGTERM sig-\\\\nnal before they are preempted by a SIGKILL, so they have\\\\ntime to clean up, save state, ﬁnish any currently-executing\\\\nrequests, and decline new ones. The actual notice may be\\\\nless if the preemptor sets a delay bound. In practice, a notice\\\\nis delivered about 80% of the time.\\\\n2.4\\\\nAllocs\\\\nA Borg alloc (short for allocation) is a reserved set of re-\\\\nsources on a machine in which one or more tasks can be\\\\nrun; the resources remain assigned whether or not they are\\\\nused. Allocs can be used to set resources aside for future\\\\ntasks, to retain resources between stopping a task and start-\\\\ning it again, and to gather tasks from different jobs onto the\\\\nsame machine – e.g., a web server instance and an associ-\\\\nated logsaver task that copies the server’s URL logs from\\\\nthe local disk to a distributed ﬁle system. The resources of\\\\nan alloc are treated in a similar way to the resources of a ma-\\\\nchine; multiple tasks running inside one share its resources.\\\\nIf an alloc must be relocated to another machine, its tasks are\\\\nrescheduled with it.\\\\nAn alloc set is like a job: it is a group of allocs that reserve\\\\nresources on multiple machines. Once an alloc set has been\\\\ncreated, one or more jobs can be submitted to run in it. For\\\\nbrevity, we will generally use “task” to refer to an alloc or a\\\\ntop-level task (one outside an alloc) and “job” to refer to a\\\\njob or alloc set.\\\\n2.5\\\\nPriority, quota, and admission control\\\\nWhat happens when more work shows up than can be ac-\\\\ncommodated? Our solutions for this are priority and quota.\\\\nEvery job has a priority, a small positive integer. A high-\\\\npriority task can obtain resources at the expense of a lower-\\\\npriority one, even if that involves preempting (killing) the\\\\nlatter. Borg deﬁnes non-overlapping priority bands for dif-\\\\nferent uses, including (in decreasing-priority order): moni-\\\\ntoring, production, batch, and best eﬀort (also known as\\\\ntesting or free). For this paper, prod jobs are the ones in the\\\\nmonitoring and production bands.\\\\nAlthough a preempted task will often be rescheduled\\\\nelsewhere in the cell, preemption cascades could occur if\\\\na high-priority task bumped out a slightly lower-priority\\\\none, which bumped out another slightly-lower priority task,\\\\nand so on. To eliminate most of this, we disallow tasks in\\\\nthe production priority band to preempt one another. Fine-\\\\ngrained priorities are still useful in other circumstances –\\\\ne.g., MapReduce master tasks run at a slightly higher priority\\\\nthan the workers they control, to improve their reliability.\\\\nPriority expresses relative importance for jobs that are\\\\nrunning or waiting to run in a cell. Quota is used to decide\\\\nwhich jobs to admit for scheduling. Quota is expressed as\\\\na vector of resource quantities (CPU, RAM, disk, etc.) at a\\\\ngiven priority, for a period of time (typically months). The\\\\nquantities specify the maximum amount of resources that\\\\na user’s job requests can ask for at a time (e.g., “20 TiB\\\\nof RAM at prod priority from now until the end of July\\\\nin cell xx”). Quota-checking is part of admission control,\\\\nnot scheduling: jobs with insufﬁcient quota are immediately\\\\nrejected upon submission.\\\\nHigher-priority quota costs more than quota at lower-\\\\npriority. Production-priority quota is limited to the actual\\\\nresources available in the cell, so that a user who submits\\\\na production-priority job that ﬁts in their quota can expect it\\\\nto run, modulo fragmentation and constraints. Even though\\\\nwe encourage users to purchase no more quota than they\\\\nneed, many users overbuy because it insulates them against\\\\nfuture shortages when their application’s user base grows.\\\\nWe respond to this by over-selling quota at lower-priority\\\\nlevels: every user has inﬁnite quota at priority zero, although\\\\nthis is frequently hard to exercise because resources are over-\\\\nsubscribed. A low-priority job may be admitted but remain\\\\npending (unscheduled) due to insufﬁcient resources.\\\\nQuota allocation is handled outside of Borg, and is inti-\\\\nmately tied to our physical capacity planning, whose results\\\\nare reﬂected in the price and availability of quota in differ-\\\\nent datacenters. User jobs are admitted only if they have suf-\\\\nﬁcient quota at the required priority. The use of quota re-\\\\nduces the need for policies like Dominant Resource Fairness\\\\n(DRF) [29, 35, 36, 66].\\\\nBorg has a capability system that gives special privileges\\\\nto some users; for example, allowing administrators to delete\\\\nor modify any job in the cell, or allowing a user to access\\\\nrestricted kernel features or Borg behaviors such as disabling\\\\nresource estimation (§5.5) on their jobs.\\\\n2.6\\\\nNaming and monitoring\\\\nIt’s not enough to create and place tasks: a service’s clients\\\\nand other systems need to be able to ﬁnd them, even after\\\\nthey are relocated to a new machine. To enable this, Borg\\\\ncreates a stable “Borg name service” (BNS) name for each\\\\ntask that includes the cell name, job name, and task number.\\\\nBorg writes the task’s hostname and port into a consistent,\\\\nhighly-available ﬁle in Chubby [14] with this name, which\\\\nis used by our RPC system to ﬁnd the task endpoint. The\\\\nBNS name also forms the basis of the task’s DNS name,\\\\nso the ﬁftieth task in job jfoo owned by user ubar in cell\\\\ncc would be reachable via 50.jfoo.ubar.cc.borg.google.com.\\\\nBorg also writes job size and task health information into\\\\nChubby whenever it changes, so load balancers can see\\\\nwhere to route requests to.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 4 ===\\\\nAlmost every task run under Borg contains a built-in\\\\nHTTP server that publishes information about the health of\\\\nthe task and thousands of performance metrics (e.g., RPC\\\\nlatencies). Borg monitors the health-check URL and restarts\\\\ntasks that do not respond promptly or return an HTTP er-\\\\nror code. Other data is tracked by monitoring tools for dash-\\\\nboards and alerts on service level objective (SLO) violations.\\\\nA service called Sigma provides a web-based user inter-\\\\nface (UI) through which a user can examine the state of all\\\\ntheir jobs, a particular cell, or drill down to individual jobs\\\\nand tasks to examine their resource behavior, detailed logs,\\\\nexecution history, and eventual fate. Our applications gener-\\\\nate voluminous logs; these are automatically rotated to avoid\\\\nrunning out of disk space, and preserved for a while after the\\\\ntask’s exit to assist with debugging. If a job is not running\\\\nBorg provides a “why pending?” annotation, together with\\\\nguidance on how to modify the job’s resource requests to\\\\nbetter ﬁt the cell. We publish guidelines for “conforming”\\\\nresource shapes that are likely to schedule easily.\\\\nBorg records all job submissions and task events, as well\\\\nas detailed per-task resource usage information in Infrastore,\\\\na scalable read-only data store with an interactive SQL-like\\\\ninterface via Dremel [61]. This data is used for usage-based\\\\ncharging, debugging job and system failures, and long-term\\\\ncapacity planning. It also provided the data for the Google\\\\ncluster workload trace [80].\\\\nAll of these features help users to understand and debug\\\\nthe behavior of Borg and their jobs, and help our SREs\\\\nmanage a few tens of thousands of machines per person.\\\\n3.\\\\nBorg architecture\\\\nA Borg cell consists of a set of machines, a logically central-\\\\nized controller called the Borgmaster, and an agent process\\\\ncalled the Borglet that runs on each machine in a cell (see\\\\nFigure 1). All components of Borg are written in C++.\\\\n3.1\\\\nBorgmaster\\\\nEach cell’s Borgmaster consists of two processes: the main\\\\nBorgmaster process and a separate scheduler (§3.2). The\\\\nmain Borgmaster process handles client RPCs that either\\\\nmutate state (e.g., create job) or provide read-only access\\\\nto data (e.g., lookup job). It also manages state machines\\\\nfor all of the objects in the system (machines, tasks, allocs,\\\\netc.), communicates with the Borglets, and offers a web UI\\\\nas a backup to Sigma.\\\\nThe Borgmaster is logically a single process but is ac-\\\\ntually replicated ﬁve times. Each replica maintains an in-\\\\nmemory copy of most of the state of the cell, and this state is\\\\nalso recorded in a highly-available, distributed, Paxos-based\\\\nstore [55] on the replicas’ local disks. A single elected mas-\\\\nter per cell serves both as the Paxos leader and the state\\\\nmutator, handling all operations that change the cell’s state,\\\\nsuch as submitting a job or terminating a task on a ma-\\\\nchine. A master is elected (using Paxos) when the cell is\\\\nbrought up and whenever the elected master fails; it acquires\\\\na Chubby lock so other systems can ﬁnd it. Electing a master\\\\nand failing-over to the new one typically takes about 10 s, but\\\\ncan take up to a minute in a big cell because some in-memory\\\\nstate has to be reconstructed. When a replica recovers from\\\\nan outage, it dynamically re-synchronizes its state from other\\\\nPaxos replicas that are up-to-date.\\\\nThe Borgmaster’s state at a point in time is called a\\\\ncheckpoint, and takes the form of a periodic snapshot plus a\\\\nchange log kept in the Paxos store. Checkpoints have many\\\\nuses, including restoring a Borgmaster’s state to an arbitrary\\\\npoint in the past (e.g., just before accepting a request that\\\\ntriggered a software defect in Borg so it can be debugged);\\\\nﬁxing it by hand in extremis; building a persistent log of\\\\nevents for future queries; and ofﬂine simulations.\\\\nA high-ﬁdelity Borgmaster simulator called Fauxmaster\\\\ncan be used to read checkpoint ﬁles, and contains a complete\\\\ncopy of the production Borgmaster code, with stubbed-out\\\\ninterfaces to the Borglets. It accepts RPCs to make state ma-\\\\nchine changes and perform operations, such as “schedule all\\\\npending tasks”, and we use it to debug failures, by interact-\\\\ning with it as if it were a live Borgmaster, with simulated\\\\nBorglets replaying real interactions from the checkpoint ﬁle.\\\\nA user can step through and observe the changes to the sys-\\\\ntem state that actually occurred in the past. Fauxmaster is\\\\nalso useful for capacity planning (“how many new jobs of\\\\nthis type would ﬁt?”), as well as sanity checks before mak-\\\\ning a change to a cell’s conﬁguration (“will this change evict\\\\nany important jobs?”).\\\\n3.2\\\\nScheduling\\\\nWhen a job is submitted, the Borgmaster records it persis-\\\\ntently in the Paxos store and adds the job’s tasks to the pend-\\\\ning queue. This is scanned asynchronously by the scheduler,\\\\nwhich assigns tasks to machines if there are sufﬁcient avail-\\\\nable resources that meet the job’s constraints. (The sched-\\\\nuler primarily operates on tasks, not jobs.) The scan pro-\\\\nceeds from high to low priority, modulated by a round-robin\\\\nscheme within a priority to ensure fairness across users and\\\\navoid head-of-line blocking behind a large job. The schedul-\\\\ning algorithm has two parts: feasibility checking, to ﬁnd ma-\\\\nchines on which the task could run, and scoring, which picks\\\\none of the feasible machines.\\\\nIn feasibility checking, the scheduler ﬁnds a set of ma-\\\\nchines that meet the task’s constraints and also have enough\\\\n“available” resources – which includes resources assigned\\\\nto lower-priority tasks that can be evicted. In scoring, the\\\\nscheduler determines the “goodness” of each feasible ma-\\\\nchine. The score takes into account user-speciﬁed prefer-\\\\nences, but is mostly driven by built-in criteria such as mini-\\\\nmizing the number and priority of preempted tasks, picking\\\\nmachines that already have a copy of the task’s packages,\\\\nspreading tasks across power and failure domains, and pack-\\\\ning quality including putting a mix of high and low priority\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 5 ===\\\\ntasks onto a single machine to allow the high-priority ones\\\\nto expand in a load spike.\\\\nBorg originally used a variant of E-PVM [4] for scoring,\\\\nwhich generates a single cost value across heterogeneous\\\\nresources and minimizes the change in cost when placing\\\\na task. In practice, E-PVM ends up spreading load across\\\\nall the machines, leaving headroom for load spikes – but at\\\\nthe expense of increased fragmentation, especially for large\\\\ntasks that need most of the machine; we sometimes call this\\\\n“worst ﬁt”.\\\\nThe opposite end of the spectrum is “best ﬁt”, which tries\\\\nto ﬁll machines as tightly as possible. This leaves some ma-\\\\nchines empty of user jobs (they still run storage servers), so\\\\nplacing large tasks is straightforward, but the tight packing\\\\npenalizes any mis-estimations in resource requirements by\\\\nusers or Borg. This hurts applications with bursty loads, and\\\\nis particularly bad for batch jobs which specify low CPU\\\\nneeds so they can schedule easily and try to run opportunis-\\\\ntically in unused resources: 20% of non-prod tasks request\\\\nless than 0.1 CPU cores.\\\\nOur current scoring model is a hybrid one that tries to\\\\nreduce the amount of stranded resources – ones that cannot\\\\nbe used because another resource on the machine is fully\\\\nallocated. It provides about 3–5% better packing efﬁciency\\\\n(deﬁned in [78]) than best ﬁt for our workloads.\\\\nIf the machine selected by the scoring phase doesn’t have\\\\nenough available resources to ﬁt the new task, Borg preempts\\\\n(kills) lower-priority tasks, from lowest to highest priority,\\\\nuntil it does. We add the preempted tasks to the scheduler’s\\\\npending queue, rather than migrate or hibernate them.3\\\\nTask startup latency (the time from job submission to\\\\na task running) is an area that has received and continues\\\\nto receive signiﬁcant attention. It is highly variable, with\\\\nthe median typically about 25 s. Package installation takes\\\\nabout 80% of the total: one of the known bottlenecks is\\\\ncontention for the local disk where packages are written to.\\\\nTo reduce task startup time, the scheduler prefers to assign\\\\ntasks to machines that already have the necessary packages\\\\n(programs and data) installed: most packages are immutable\\\\nand so can be shared and cached. (This is the only form of\\\\ndata locality supported by the Borg scheduler.) In addition,\\\\nBorg distributes packages to machines in parallel using tree-\\\\nand torrent-like protocols.\\\\nAdditionally, the scheduler uses several techniques to let\\\\nit scale up to cells with tens of thousands of machines (§3.4).\\\\n3.3\\\\nBorglet\\\\nThe Borglet is a local Borg agent that is present on every\\\\nmachine in a cell. It starts and stops tasks; restarts them if\\\\nthey fail; manages local resources by manipulating OS ker-\\\\nnel settings; rolls over debug logs; and reports the state of the\\\\nmachine to the Borgmaster and other monitoring systems.\\\\n3 Exception: tasks that provide virtual machines for Google Compute En-\\\\ngine users are migrated.\\\\nThe Borgmaster polls each Borglet every few seconds to\\\\nretrieve the machine’s current state and send it any outstand-\\\\ning requests. This gives Borgmaster control over the rate of\\\\ncommunication, avoids the need for an explicit ﬂow control\\\\nmechanism, and prevents recovery storms [9].\\\\nThe elected master is responsible for preparing messages\\\\nto send to the Borglets and for updating the cell’s state with\\\\ntheir responses. For performance scalability, each Borgmas-\\\\nter replica runs a stateless link shard to handle the communi-\\\\ncation with some of the Borglets; the partitioning is recalcu-\\\\nlated whenever a Borgmaster election occurs. For resiliency,\\\\nthe Borglet always reports its full state, but the link shards\\\\naggregate and compress this information by reporting only\\\\ndifferences to the state machines, to reduce the update load\\\\nat the elected master.\\\\nIf a Borglet does not respond to several poll messages its\\\\nmachine is marked as down and any tasks it was running\\\\nare rescheduled on other machines. If communication is\\\\nrestored the Borgmaster tells the Borglet to kill those tasks\\\\nthat have been rescheduled, to avoid duplicates. A Borglet\\\\ncontinues normal operation even if it loses contact with the\\\\nBorgmaster, so currently-running tasks and services stay up\\\\neven if all Borgmaster replicas fail.\\\\n3.4\\\\nScalability\\\\nWe are not sure where the ultimate scalability limit to Borg’s\\\\ncentralized architecture will come from; so far, every time\\\\nwe have approached a limit, we’ve managed to eliminate it.\\\\nA single Borgmaster can manage many thousands of ma-\\\\nchines in a cell, and several cells have arrival rates above\\\\n10 000 tasks per minute. A busy Borgmaster uses 10–14\\\\nCPU cores and up to 50 GiB RAM. We use several tech-\\\\nniques to achieve this scale.\\\\nEarly versions of Borgmaster had a simple, synchronous\\\\nloop that accepted requests, scheduled tasks, and commu-\\\\nnicated with Borglets. To handle larger cells, we split the\\\\nscheduler into a separate process so it could operate in paral-\\\\nlel with the other Borgmaster functions that are replicated for\\\\nfailure tolerance. A scheduler replica operates on a cached\\\\ncopy of the cell state. It repeatedly: retrieves state changes\\\\nfrom the elected master (including both assigned and pend-\\\\ning work); updates its local copy; does a scheduling pass\\\\nto assign tasks; and informs the elected master of those as-\\\\nsignments. The master will accept and apply these assign-\\\\nments unless they are inappropriate (e.g., based on out of\\\\ndate state), which will cause them to be reconsidered in the\\\\nscheduler’s next pass. This is quite similar in spirit to the\\\\noptimistic concurrency control used in Omega [69], and in-\\\\ndeed we recently added the ability for Borg to use different\\\\nschedulers for different workload types.\\\\nTo improve response times, we added separate threads\\\\nto talk to the Borglets and respond to read-only RPCs. For\\\\ngreater performance, we sharded (partitioned) these func-\\\\ntions across the ﬁve Borgmaster replicas §3.3. Data from August 1st 2013.\\\\nthese keep the 99%ile response time of the UI below 1 s\\\\nand the 95%ile of the Borglet polling interval below 10 s.\\\\nSeveral things make the Borg scheduler more scalable:\\\\nScore caching: Evaluating feasibility and scoring a ma-\\\\nchine is expensive, so Borg caches the scores until the prop-\\\\nerties of the machine or task change – e.g., a task on the ma-\\\\nchine terminates, an attribute is altered, or a task’s require-\\\\nments change. Ignoring small changes in resource quantities\\\\nreduces cache invalidations.\\\\nEquivalence classes: Tasks in a Borg job usually have\\\\nidentical requirements and constraints, so rather than deter-\\\\nmining feasibility for every pending task on every machine,\\\\nand scoring all the feasible machines, Borg only does fea-\\\\nsibility and scoring for one task per equivalence class – a\\\\ngroup of tasks with identical requirements.\\\\nRelaxed randomization: It is wasteful to calculate fea-\\\\nsibility and scores for all the machines in a large cell, so the\\\\nscheduler examines machines in a random order until it has\\\\nfound “enough” feasible machines to score, and then selects\\\\nthe best within that set. The data was\\\\ngathered from ∼12000 randomly selected prod tasks over\\\\na week, counting cycles and instructions over a 5 minute in-\\\\nterval using the hardware proﬁling infrastructure described\\\\nin [83], and weighting samples so that every second of CPU\\\\ntime is counted equally. The limit is used\\\\nby Borg to determine if the user has enough quota to admit\\\\nthe job, and to determine if a particular machine has enough\\\\nfree resources to schedule the task. Just as there are users\\\\nwho buy more quota than they need, there are users who\\\\nrequest more resources than their tasks will use, because\\\\nBorg will normally kill a task that tries to use more RAM\\\\nor disk space than it requested, or throttle CPU to what it\\\\nasked for. In addition, some tasks occasionally need to use\\\\nall their resources (e.g., at peak times of day or while coping\\\\nwith a denial-of-service attack), but most of the time do not.\\\\nRather than waste allocated resources that are not cur-\\\\nrently being consumed, we estimate how many resources a\\\\ntask will use and reclaim the rest for work that can tolerate\\\\nlower-quality resources, such as batch jobs. This whole pro-\\\\ncess is called resource reclamation. The estimate is called\\\\nthe task’s reservation, and is computed by the Borgmas-\\\\nter every few seconds, using ﬁne-grained usage (resource-\\\\nconsumption) information captured by the Borglet. The ini-\\\\ntial reservation is set equal to the resource request (the limit);\\\\nafter 300 s, to allow for startup transients, it decays slowly\\\\ntowards the actual usage plus a safety margin. The reserva-\\\\ntion is rapidly increased if the usage exceeds it.\\\\nThe Borg scheduler uses limits to calculate feasibility\\\\n(§3.2) for prod tasks,4 so they never rely on reclaimed re-\\\\nsources and aren’t exposed to resource oversubscription; for\\\\nnon-prod tasks, it uses the reservations of existing tasks so\\\\nthe new tasks can be scheduled into reclaimed resources.\\\\nA machine may run out of resources at runtime if the\\\\nreservations (predictions) are wrong – even if all tasks use\\\\n4 To be precise, high-priority latency-sensitive ones – see §6.2.\\\\n0−20%\\\\n20−40% 40−60% 60−80% 80−100%\\\\n0%\\\\n1%\\\\n2%\\\\n3%\\\\n4%\\\\nMachine CPU utilization\\\\n \\\\n \\\\n[10ms, inf)\\\\n[5ms, 10ms)\\\\n[1ms, 5ms)\\\\nFigure 13: Scheduling delays as a function of load.
